title: GPU memory slice allocator: dynamic budgeting for weights / KV / activations under continuous batching
creator: Maya Patel
description: Background: Continuous batching and large KV caches are critical for throughput, but they compete with model weights and activation buffers for limited GPU memory. Recent spikes in multi-tenant workloads show transient OOMs when batched request tail lengths and KV occupancy align. This ticket implements a per-GPU dynamic memory 'slice allocator' that maintains explicit budgets for three primary consumers: model weights (including checkpoints/quantized variants), KV cache (per-tenant prefix caches), and activation/batching buffers. Goal: avoid OOMs and minimize conservative over-provisioning while preserving throughput/latency targets.
design_summary: We will introduce a lightweight resident budget table per GPU with three adjustable reservations: W(weights), K(KV), A(activations). The allocator enforces soft caps and a fast pre-check on allocation requests. If allocations would violate soft caps, the allocator attempts: 1) eviction of low-reuse KV entries (LRU with reuse score), 2) compacting activation buffers (reduce temporary workspace where safe), 3) fall back to an emergency reserve pool (configurable headroom) or degrade to a smaller model variant. The system ties into the routing policy to throttle or redirect requests when memory pressure persists. A background sampler estimates expected KV tail growth using recent per-tenant seq-length distributions to adjust K dynamically.
metrics: Primary: OOM rate (per-GPU/day), tail latency (95/99p), throughput (tokens/sec), average GPU memory utilization broken down by consumer (W/K/A), cost-per-token. Secondary: KV eviction churn, number of fallbacks to smaller model variants.
tradeoffs_and_risks: - Over-reserving K reduces throughput if activations need space; under-reserving causes OOMs. - Evicting KV hurts quality (longer prefix leads to degraded generation) and increases CPU/GPU overhead on cache reloads. - Adding complexity to allocator increases risk of regressions in the runtime path; keep fast path microbenchmarked. - Emergency fallback to smaller models impacts latency/quality and must be signaled upstream.
implementation_plan: 1) Prototype a budget table and allocator in a feature branch (runtime/memory-slice) with unit tests. 2) Implement KV reuse scorer and fast eviction API. 3) Add activation workspace compaction hooks for popular kernels. 4) Integrate sampler that observes seq-length distributions and updates recommended K. 5) Build simulation harness to replay production traces and validate headroom policies. 6) Expose knobs to routing layer and Console for SLO-driven headroom tuning.
simulation_results_summary: Initial local simulator (toy traces) shows that a 7% headroom reserve with adaptive K reduces OOMs by ~92% vs no headroom and reduces mean wasted reserved memory by ~45% compared to static 20% safety margin. Multi-tenant replay (in progress) indicates one tenant pattern still forces frequent KV churn; plan is targeted tenant throttling in that case.
rollout_plan: - Phase 1: deploy prototype behind runtime flag on canary pool; monitor OOMs and tail latency for 48h. - Phase 2: expand to 10% of serving capacity with gradual K tuning from sampler recommendations. - Phase 3: full rollout with Console defaults and per-customer overrides.
monitoring_and_alerting: New dashboards: per-GPU memory breakdown (weights/KV/activations), headroom consumption, eviction rate, fallback count. Alerts: OOM spike (>3/min for a GPU), eviction-churn alert, repeated fallback to smaller model (>5/hr for a route).
acceptance_criteria: - No increase in client-visible 99p latency after Phase 2. - OOM rate decreases or stays flat in canary pool. - Eviction churn remains below threshold for 95% of tenants. - Console shows accurate breakdown and knobs for K and headroom.
qa_plan: Unit tests for allocator fast path and eviction policy. Integration tests using synthetic workloads with controlled seq-length distributions. Replayer-based stress tests using anonymized production traces in staging GPUs. Canary rollout with detailed telemetry and rollback flag.
